title: Chapter 79 — Habits and the Inner Game
intro: Preparation beats luck. Consistency beats talent. Habits beat intentions. This chapter is about the work nobody sees that creates the results everybody notices.

sections.title: You Are Not Lucky — You Are Prepared
sections.content:
Luck is one of the most overused explanations in sales. People say 'they got the good customer' or 'they were lucky' or 'the customer walked right to them.'

Over a week, luck may influence results. Over a year, habits determine results.

Luck favours the prepared mind. Preparation means knowing your inventory, knowing what is in stock, understanding promotions, knowing financing options, learning new products, practicing presentations, reviewing objections, following up with past customers, building your CRM, and improving every day.

Prepared people recognize opportunities that unprepared people never even notice. The customer who casually mentions a renovation is an opportunity for five appliances — but only if you are listening, and only if you know what questions to ask next.

sections.title: What Downtime Actually Costs You
sections.content:
One of the biggest differences between average and elite salespeople is how they use the quiet moments between customers.

Average salespeople spend downtime complaining, gossiping, looking at their phones, and waiting for the next customer to walk through the door.

Elite salespeople spend downtime calling previous customers, following up on quotes, checking deliveries, confirming orders, learning product updates, practicing presentations, cleaning up CRM records, building referrals, and reviewing inventory.

Customers only see a few minutes of your work. Your income is built during the hours between those conversations.

If you have ten people on a sales floor and one is making $200,000 a year while another is making $60,000 — same floor, same product, same customers — the difference is not talent and it is not luck. It is what they do when nobody is watching.

sections.title: Never Stop Learning
sections.content:
Experience never replaces learning. Even after decades in the industry, there is always something worth reviewing.

I have been in appliances for 20 years. I have been to probably thousands of manufacturer trainings. I know the majority of everything they teach. But I always forget at least one thing, and they remind me when I am there. Even if I learn nothing new, a feature I forgot or a feature I missed from the last training comes back.

Doctors continue medical education. Lawyers study new legislation. Teachers complete professional development. Engineers maintain certifications. Pilots train constantly. These professionals make hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. You are no different. Your potential in a commission sales environment is equivalent to theirs — with a great database and the right habits.

Professional salespeople should treat learning as part of the job, not something extra.

sections.title: Breaking a Sales Slump
sections.content:
Every salesperson experiences slumps. Even the highest performers have days, weeks, or even months where nothing seems to go their way. Customers disappear. Quotes do not come back. Deals fall apart. Referrals dry up.

The difference between average and elite salespeople is not that they avoid slumps. It is how they respond to them.

When results decline, many salespeople immediately blame the economy, bad customers, pricing, competition, marketing, or luck. While those factors can affect individual sales, they rarely explain a prolonged decline.

The first place to look is always yourself. Not because you are at fault — but because you are the one thing you can control.

sections.title: Return to the 10 Steps
sections.content:
When you are struggling, do not create a new sales process. Go back to the fundamentals.

Mentally review every customer interaction. Ask yourself honestly:

Did I build rapport?
Did I complete a thorough discovery?
Did I truly understand their needs?
Did I uncover their wants?
Did I present the right solution?
Did I demonstrate the product properly?
Did I answer every objection?
Did I confidently ask for the sale?
Did I explain the next steps clearly?
Did I follow up?

Small shortcuts often create big losses. And the shortcut that kills more sales than any other is skipping or rushing through discovery.

sections.title: The Most Common Slump Problem
sections.content:
In my experience, the issue usually is not lack of product knowledge. It is becoming too comfortable.

Experienced salespeople sometimes begin to rush the presentation, assume they know what the customer wants, skip discovery, skip demonstrations, talk more than they listen, answer questions before understanding the problem, and assume the customer already knows the benefits.

Experience can become a strength or a weakness. Confidence is valuable. Assumptions are expensive.

The best fix is surprisingly simple. Slow down. Listen more. Talk less. Customers rarely buy because they heard the most words. They buy because they felt understood.

Remember — you may have sold thousands of appliances. Your customer probably has not bought one in years. What feels obvious to you may be completely new to them. Never skip an explanation because it seems basic. Customers do not need you to impress them with knowledge. They need you to make a complicated purchase feel simple and comfortable.

sections.title: Use Every Slump as Feedback
sections.content:
Sales slumps are not failures. They are feedback. Treat them like a dashboard warning light.

Instead of asking 'why is nobody buying?' ask 'which part of my process has slipped?'

Small corrections made early prevent long-term declines. The 10 Steps are not just a way to make a sale — they are a diagnostic tool. If one step is weak, the entire sale becomes harder.

Elite salespeople do not become great because they never struggle. They become great because they notice when their standards begin to slip and correct themselves before bad habits become permanent.

Whenever results decline, resist the urge to reinvent your approach. Return to the fundamentals. The basics built your success in the first place. They will usually rebuild it.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating habits and inner game, ask:

Does the salesperson use downtime productively or waste it?
Are they continuously learning or have they become comfortable with what they already know?
Do they manage their CRM proactively or reactively?
When results decline, do they inspect their own process first — or blame external factors?
Can they identify which of the 10 Steps has slipped during a cold stretch?
Do they treat learning as part of the job or as optional?

Preparation beats luck. Consistency beats talent. Habits beat intentions. The best salespeople do not hope for opportunities. They prepare for them before they arrive.
